nameStory: Staurodesmus octocornis gets its scientific name from Greek words meaning 'cross-shaped' (stauros) and 'bond' (desmus), referring to how these microscopic algae often link together. The species name 'octocornis' means 'eight-horned,' describing the eight spiny projections that make this tiny organism look like a medieval star weapon under the microscope.
description: This is a single-celled freshwater alga so small you'd need a microscope to see it properly - each cell is only about 1/100th of a millimeter across! It has a distinctive star-like shape with eight pointed spines radiating outward, and a narrow waist in the middle that gives it an hourglass appearance. Like other desmids (des-mids), it's bright green due to chlorophyll and often links up with others to form short chains. You'll find it floating in clean ponds and lakes throughout New England.

idTips.label: Eight radiating spines
idTips.description: The cell has exactly eight sharp, pointed projections extending outward like spokes on a wheel - this is the key identifying feature that separates it from other desmids

idTips.label: Constricted middle
idTips.description: The cell pinches inward at its center, creating a narrow waist between two semicircular halves that looks like an hourglass or figure-eight shape

idTips.label: Bright green color
idTips.description: The cell appears vivid emerald green under magnification due to its chloroplasts, which may show as distinct oval patches within each cell half

idTips.label: Microscopic size
idTips.description: Individual cells are extremely tiny at roughly 10-20 micrometers, invisible to the naked eye and requiring at least 400x magnification to see clearly

habitat: Found in clean, unpolluted freshwater environments including mountain ponds, clear lakes, and slow-moving streams throughout New England's forests and mountains. It prefers slightly acidic water with low nutrient levels, often appearing in the same pristine waters where you'd find native brook trout. Most commonly discovered in higher elevation waters and bog pools where water quality remains excellent.

seasonality.spring: Populations begin growing as ice melts and water temperatures rise, often most abundant during late spring when nutrients from snowmelt are available but competition from other algae is still low.
seasonality.summer: Peak abundance occurs in midsummer, especially in cooler mountain lakes where water temperatures remain moderate and oxygen levels stay high.
seasonality.fall: Still present but declining numbers as temperatures drop and daylight hours decrease, though they may persist longer in warmer, protected water bodies.
seasonality.winter: Survives under ice in dormant stages, with very low activity levels until spring warmth returns to trigger new growth cycles.

funFact: Despite being a single cell smaller than the width of a human hair, Staurodesmus octocornis is considered an excellent 'canary in the coal mine' for water quality - scientists use its presence to indicate that a lake or pond is still pristine and unpolluted, since even small amounts of pollution will cause it to disappear completely.
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other spiny desmids, but the exact count of eight spines is diagnostic - count carefully since related species have different numbers of projections. Remember 'octo-cornis' means eight horns, just like an octopus has eight arms.
contextualKnowledge: The name 'desmid' comes from Greek meaning 'little chain,' referring to how many species link together, though this particular species is more often found as single cells. These microscopic algae are completely unrelated to the large seaweeds most people think of as 'algae' - they're actually more closely related to land plants.
compareHints: Unlike Staurodesmus triangularis which has three main projections, or S. longispinus with its extremely long spines, octocornis always has exactly eight moderately-sized spines of roughly equal length. It's larger and more robust than S. brevispina (short-spined) but smaller than the massive S. validus, and its spines are straighter and more regularly arranged than the curved projections of S. convergens.
